title: Accessible column-snaplines and user-density-presets for virtual table layouts
creator: Ava Martinez
description:
Problem: Our virtualized table supports column resizing and density modes, but the current gestures are hard to discover, fragile for keyboard users, and produce inconsistent layouts across devices. Users asked for easier alignment between columns when switching densities, predictable snap behaviour, and a way to save their preferred density + column widths per user.

Goal: Design an accessible, keyboard-first column-resize experience that includes visible 'snaplines' (magnetized alignment guides) that are density-aware, and a per-user density preset mechanism that persists layouts across sessions and devices. The solution should: explain visual language, keyboard affordances, saving semantics, and migration strategy for existing persisted layouts.
acceptance_criteria: Keyboard-first resize: users can focus a column separator and press arrow keys to nudge width; Shift for 10px increments; Enter commits a snap when within snapline threshold
Snaplines: visual guides appear when a resize or density change would align a column with a recommended breakpoint or neighboring column; snapline outline + subtle pulse animation for 150ms
Density-aware alignment: when switching density modes (compact/regular/comfortable), columns attempt to preserve proportional widths where feasible and indicate collisions with a transient overlay
Persisted presets: user can save a named layout (density + column widths + pinned columns) to their profile; saved presets sync via server and appear on other devices
Fallback: if server sync is unavailable, localStorage fallback persists last-customized layout with clear UI state indicating unsynced changes
A11y: screen reader announcements for resize start/stop/current-width and when a snap occurs; visible focus ring and 1:1 keyboard parity with mouse/trackpad
Developer hooks: resize telemetry events and an opt-in "layout-change" analytics event; API surface notes for engineers
design_decisions: Persist to server vs local only: choose server persistence by default for cross-device sync; fall back to localStorage. Rationale: users expect settings to follow them across machines and workspaces.
Snap thresholds: use proportional threshold (2.5% of table width) rather than fixed px to handle small/large viewports. Rationale: consistent feel across devices and responsive layouts.
Visual language: snaplines are 1px high, 40% opaque accent color with short pulsing highlight. Use motion token for 150ms to avoid motion sickness. Rationale: balance discoverability and subtlety.
Keyboard increments: arrow keys = 1px nudge; Shift+arrow = 10px; Cmd/Meta+arrow = snap to next major breakpoint. Rationale: fine + coarse control for power users.

Accessibility: announce "Column resize started" on focus activation, announce width updates on change, and announce "snapped to breakpoint" when snap occurs. Rationale: parity for screen reader users.

Migration: existing persisted layouts will be converted with a migration script that maps prior width units to proportional widths and marks migrated presets as 'legacy' for user review. Rationale: avoid layout corruption across older saved states.
tradeoffs: Server persistence increases backend work and introduces sync complexity; tradeoff accepted for cross-device UX and enterprise expectation.
Proportional snap threshold avoids odd behavior on very narrow tables but can be unintuitive for extreme zoom levels; will add a UI hint and tooltip on first use.
Adding snapline animations increases rendering work in the runtime; design favors a low-cost pulse and leverage existing motion tokens to minimize perf impact.
comments: 2025-02-13 - Ava Martinez: Initial sketch and problem framing added. Called out need for migration with ENG and PM. Filed ENG-32788 for backend API endpoints.
2025-02-18 - Jonah Patel: Wireframes in Figma updated with keyboard flows. Noted edge-case when many columns pinned and proportional scaling collides. Asked for a visual for 'collision overlay'.

Prototype keyboard flows in Storybook and run a small usability test with 6 users (keyboard-first) by 2025-03-12
risks: Backend sync delays causing conflicting presets; mitigation: optimistic UI and versioned presets with conflict resolution prompt
Large-table perf regressions if we recalc proportional widths on every frame; mitigation: throttle and compute diffs only for changed columns
Privacy: saved layouts may reveal column choices that include PII-sensitive column IDs; mitigation: server stores layout with stable column keys and RBAC check before exposing layouts across orgs
